title: Placerville Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Placerville wells have a 143-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock makes yield and drilling cost variable.
h1: Placerville Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Placerville show a mountain setting where most wells are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Of the 678 permitted wells in the Colorado DWR records, 400 are recorded as constructed and 432 report a total depth.

The numbers give a useful starting point, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Nearby records include wells from 50 to 1,210 feet, and only 161 report a pump yield. A site-specific bid should account for access, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, and the chance that fractured rock produces less water than a nearby well.

sections.heading: Placerville well depth depends on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median well depth near Placerville is 143 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 320 feet, so a driller bidding a typical home site should not assume every well will resemble the median. The depth distribution is broad: 41% are under 100 feet, 28% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 23% between 300 and 600 feet, and 8% reach 600 feet or more.

The deepest recorded well is 1,210 feet. That spread is consistent with fractured granite and gneiss, where water-bearing fractures may be shallow on one parcel and much deeper on another. Before buying, compare completed wells on the same slope, road, or drainage rather than relying only on the countywide median.

sections.heading: What Placerville wells usually produce
sections.html:
Among the 161 nearby records that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 5.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute, which is a workable range for many household uses when the well, pressure system, storage, and permitted use are properly matched.

Reported production is not uniform. 65% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 17% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 17% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the well test, not just a verbal estimate. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but it can affect design and cost.

sections.heading: Water levels near Placerville show little decade change
sections.html:
The median static water level is 62 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 24 to 171 feet. Static level means the water in the well when it is not being pumped; it is not the same as the total drilled depth or the available household supply.

The reported decade medians are nearly unchanged: 53 feet below surface in the 2010s and 54 feet in the 2020s. That limited record does not suggest a clear broad decline, but only 44 wells report a static water level. Seasonal conditions, pumping, elevation, and the connected fracture system can still matter at an individual property. Have the seller provide recent production and water-level information where available.

sections.heading: Placerville permit history and the drillers in the records
sections.html:
Placerville’s well history is concentrated in permits issued from the 1980s through the 2000s: 111 in the 1980s, 218 in the 1990s, and 123 in the 2000s. There are also 48 permits from the 2010s and 42 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) with 117 records, Western Drilling Services, LLC (Kuchler, Richard A.) with 104, and Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth) with 77. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and the full scope of any bid.

sections.heading: What a new Placerville well may cost
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss, the drilling model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 143 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $9,300 to $14,300. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $15,300 to $26,300 at the median depth. The middle-half depth range of 50 to 320 feet explains why two nearby lots can receive very different bids. Ask whether the proposal includes casing, grout, mobilization, access, water testing, pump sizing, and an allowance for additional footage. In fractured rock, the final cost can rise if the first water-bearing fractures do not provide enough yield.

sections.heading: Placerville risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Permit records show that 75% of wells are for domestic or household use, with 7% for stock, 1% for irrigation, and 20% for monitoring. A household-use well is generally an exempt well, but the permit controls the allowed use and pumping conditions. Colorado’s exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute; do not assume a permit supports irrigation, additional dwellings, or other expanded uses.

Environmental screening should include 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 91 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site mapped within about 10 miles. Test well water for the risks relevant to the parcel. Check septic setbacks, surface drainage, access for a rig, and the building site before drilling. Low yield, a dry hole, poor casing or grout, and difficult trenching can all affect the project.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Placerville, Sawpit, and Telluride
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then review DWR permits and construction reports for neighboring wells. Records near Placerville include the nearby area of Sawpit, as well as Mountain Village, Telluride, Ophir, Norwood, and Ridgway. The closest comparison is usually more useful than an average taken across the entire county, especially in fractured bedrock.

For a purchase, make the well permit, construction report, yield test, static level, water-quality results, and septic approval part of due diligence. For a new build, obtain a driller’s access and depth estimate before finalizing the house location. Confirm the planned use with Colorado DWR, design storage if the yield calls for it, and budget beyond the median. The records show useful water in many wells, but they do not remove parcel-by-parcel uncertainty.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Placerville, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Placerville is 143 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 320 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 1,210 feet. Because the local aquifer is commonly fractured bedrock, depth can change sharply between nearby parcels. Use neighboring construction reports to refine a drilling estimate.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Placerville?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 143-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,300 to $14,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,300 to $26,300. Extra depth, access, and low yield can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Placerville?
faq.a: Among 161 records reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. About 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 17% report more than 15 gallons per minute. A well test is more useful for a property than the regional median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Placerville?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, records map 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 91 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the property’s water for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and maintain the well, casing, grout, and septic system.

faq.q: Are Placerville well water levels going down?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 53 feet below surface in the 2010s and 54 feet in the 2020s, which does not show a clear broad decline. However, only 44 wells report static water levels, so the series is limited. A parcel’s elevation, fractures, season, pumping, and well construction can produce a different result.
